The trumpet is the highest-sounding instrument in the brass family. Its sound starts with your **lips buzzing** in a cup-shaped mouthpiece.
This page follows a teacher's resource book (see the Works Cited), in this site's own words. For the fingerings, go to the
[Trumpet, Euphonium and Tuba fingering charts](brass-fingerings.qmd).

## Where it came from {#history}

- Trumpets of one kind or another are **over 3,000 years old**. The earliest were bronze and silver and were probably **signals** for religion or war.
- In the **Middle Ages** the trumpet was tied to the military and to pomp. Trumpeters were **guarded heavily** in battle because armies relied on them to pass on orders.
  Around then the old **six-foot straight tube with a flared bell** was bent into a wide **"S"**. By the **1500s** it was three straight lengths joined by U-shaped bends.
- By the **Baroque period** it was a single coiled tube **without valves**, the **natural trumpet**, and composers loved it. The Baroque is called the
  **Golden Age of the natural trumpet**.
- **Valves** arrived in **1815**. The trumpet became a **three-valve** instrument that could play every note of the chromatic scale. But the trumpet was slow to take up valves,
  and much early music by Mozart, Beethoven and Brahms was still written for the natural trumpet.
- For about the next **100 years** the **cornet**, which used valves, was the preferred solo instrument. In the **20th century** more music was written for the trumpet again.

## The trumpet family {#family}

| Instrument | What the book says |
|---|---|
| **B♭ trumpet** | **Cylindrical bore** and usually a **shallower mouthpiece cup**: a **bright** sound. The most common trumpet, used in most school bands and orchestras. |
| **C trumpet** | The choice of most **professional orchestral** players, because it makes **sharp keys easier**. |
| **Piccolo trumpet** | Sounds an **octave higher** than the B♭ trumpet. Light, very distinct tone; a **solo** instrument, often used for **Baroque** solos. |
| **Cornet** | **Conical bore**, a **deeper-cupped** mouthpiece, and a **mellower** tone than the trumpet. |
| **Flugelhorn** | On the book's fingering chart it shares the B♭ trumpet and cornet fingerings. Its description is on pages not in the scan. |

## Mouthpieces {#mouthpieces}

- **Vincent Bach** numbering has long been the standard. The **number is the cup's diameter: lower number = wider cup**. A Bach 3 is wider than a Bach 10½.
  Cup width mostly decides **how big the sound** is. Your lips vibrate against each other like a **double reed**, so a cup that does not fit your lips weakens the buzz.
- The **letter** after the number often gives the **cup depth** (not every maker follows this). In Bach mouthpieces **A is the deepest and E the shallowest**.
  **Deep cups: fuller, darker. Shallow cups: lighter, brighter.** Cornet and flugelhorn mouthpieces are usually deeper.
- **Rim.** A **wide** rim is comfortable but **deadens** the sound and limits flexibility. A **rounded** rim feels good but can make **tonguing less clear**; a **sharper** edge
  tongues more clearly but **tires** you faster. Something in between is usually best.
- **Throat.** A **large** throat darkens the sound; a **small** one brightens it.
- **Beginners** should choose a **medium** cup diameter, depth, throat and rim, and move to a **larger** cup as the embouchure gets stronger.
  The book suggests **Bach 7C** or **Schilke #11 or #12** for beginners and **Bach 3C or 1C** or **Schilke #14 or #20** later.

## Mutes {#mutes}

- Every mute **changes the tone colour** and **lowers the volume** a little, so you may need to play a bit louder.
- Most mutes make the trumpet play **sharper**, more in the **low register** than the middle or high. Pull the **tuning slide out about a quarter inch** when you put a mute in,
  and **push it back** when you take it out.
- The common ones: **straight, cup, harmon, bucket, plunger and derby**. A harmon mute can be played with or without its **stem** (usually **without** in jazz).
- If the music does not name a mute, use the **straight mute**. In a section, **everyone uses the same mute** so the sound matches.

## The parts {#parts}

**Mouthpiece** (with its **shank**), **mouthpiece receiver** and **lead pipe**, the **body**, **first, second and third valves**, the **hook** (finger hook), the **third valve ring**,
**first, second and third valve slides**, the **tuning slide**, the **water key** and the **bell**.

## Is it the right instrument for you? {#selecting}

The book lists these for a successful trumpeter: **thin to medium lips** (thick lips suit trombone, baritone and tuba better), **straight, even front teeth** that close evenly,
**able to sing a common folk song**, a high level of **confidence**, strong **work habits** and achievement, and strong **parental support**.

## Putting it together and holding it {#posture}

**Assembly.** Put the mouthpiece in the lead pipe's receiver and give it a **gentle twist**, not too tight.

**Posture and hands.**

1. Sit **up straight at the edge of the chair**, feet flat on the floor.
2. **Left hand**: fingers around the **third valve casing**, thumb around the **first valve casing**; put your **ring finger or middle finger in the third valve ring**.
3. **Right thumb** under the lead pipe, between the first and second valves.
4. **Fingertips of your first three right-hand fingers** on the valve buttons; the hand makes a relaxed **"C"**, as if holding a tennis ball.
5. Right **little finger on top of the hook** (not in it). Keep both **wrists straight**, tilt the instrument slightly to the right, and keep the **elbows away from your body**.

## Your embouchure and first sound {#embouchure}

1. **Wet your lips** and shape the mouth and throat as if saying **"oh"**. Bring the lips together as if saying **"em"**.
2. Take a **full breath through the mouth** and blow through closed lips: a **relaxed buzz**.
3. Take the mouthpiece off, hold it by the **shank** and set it **over the middle of the buzz**, equal on upper and lower lip, **without much pressure**. **Use a mirror.**
4. Breathe in fully and play a **long, steady buzz** on the mouthpiece.

## When the tone goes wrong {#tone-problems}

| What you hear | Possible causes | Try this |
|---|---|---|
| 1. No tone, rushing air | lips not together; too much pucker; blowing, not buzzing; dry lips or mouthpiece; not enough air | re-form the "em" position; buzz without the mouthpiece; lick the lips and the inside of the mouthpiece; breathe fully and use faster air |
| 2. Airy tone (some airiness is normal until the lip begins to vibrate on its own) | lips not together; too much pucker | re-form and hold the "em" position |
| 3. Tight, thin, pinched tone | tense, over-pursed lips (biting); too much pucker; tight closed throat | relax and re-form "em" with less pursing; no pucker; breathe and try a yawn with the head up |
| 4. Stopped sound (restricted throat or buzz) | tense, over-pursed lips; too much mouthpiece pressure; tight closed throat | relax; relax the left-hand grip and **take the right little finger out of the hook**; breathe and yawn with the head up |

## Tuning {#tuning}

- A good **tone** comes first: "you can't tune a poor tone".
- **Slur up to a tuning note** (the book prints one for beginners and one for more advanced players) so your embouchure stays natural. **Sharp**: pull the tuning slide **out**. **Flat**: push it **in**.
- Some notes are **naturally out of tune** on most trumpets: the book shows a group of **low notes that tend to be very sharp**, a group in the middle that tend to be **sharp** and a few that tend to be **flat**.
- Like every valved instrument, the trumpet has trouble when valves are **used together**. The book says **1 + 3** and **1 + 2 + 3** sound **sharp**: **extend the third valve slide** to lower them.
  How far depends on the trumpet, so **listen**. (This is the footnote on the fingering chart: "move the third valve slide out for low D and C♯".)

## Daily care {#care}

**Putting it away.** Press the **water key** and **blow** (not buzz) to empty the water. **Wipe** the trumpet with a soft, clean cloth. **Push in all the slides**, pressing the matching valve each time.
Take out the mouthpiece and put it in the case. Put the trumpet in with the **second valve slide facing up**. Latch the case.

**Oiling the valves (daily).** Unscrew **only the first valve** at the top of its casing (not the button) and do not touch the part the casing protects. Put **4 or 5 drops** of valve oil along the
metal part with the holes. Put it back, turn the button **clockwise** until it **clicks**, and screw the valve in. Push the button up and down quickly. Repeat with valves two and three.

**Greasing the slides (regularly).** See the [euphonium page](euphonium.qmd#care): the steps are the same one slide at a time.
